title: Pulse X
label: Inspired Sounds
release_date: 2002 (Wikipedia: first 12" in March 2002, wider release 8 July 2002)
tracklist_note: Instrumental. 2015 White Peach reissue EP (WPR007, 12" ltd 500 + digital): Pulse X / Revival / Formula / Formula 2.

sound_descriptions.text: A single 16-bar loop: first 8 bars in a 2-step garage style, second 8 bars stripped to kick and snare; no intro, fade-out ending; a voice sample recurs every 32 bars at the switch.
Stripped down to overdriven bass bleeps and handclaps; lo-fi and minimal with large empty spaces.
Breakbeat garage deconstructed into a minimal, twisted loop.
Producer says he programmed the drum pattern in Propellerhead ReBirth, then sampled a bassline, sequencing in Digital Orchestrator.

context.text: Ranked no. 1 in FACT's 'The 20 best Grime records ever made' (credited Musical Mob, Inspired Sounds, 2002).

Widely considered the first grime beat / a 'year zero'; its minimalism credited with making grime more MC-centred. Bok Bok named it his favourite example of Youngstar's 'simplistic, brutalist genius' (2014).
Ransom Note interview describes it as 'the first 8 bar track released' and says it sold out within its first week at Blackmarket (record shop); sold heavily on vinyl.
SPIN (Philip Sherburne, 2012) argues it as grime's founding track, noting Wiley's 'Eskimo' as the rival contender later in 2002.

relationships.other: Musical Mob - Pulse Y / Pulse Xtra / Pulse XYZ / Pulse 2005
Bring Back the Ladies (Pulse X Vocal Mix), vocals by Lorraine Cato
Wiley - Pulse Eskimo (aka Gun Shot Riddim)
Pulse X remixes by Visionist, Blackwax, Slackk, Pedro 123, Elsewhere
Mystry - Pulse 8 (opening beat on JME's Integrity>, 2015)

Credit appears as Musical Mob on early pressings (FACT) and Youngstar on later reissues. title: I Luv U
label: XL Recordings (official single); earlier test pressing
format: Test pressing circulated on pirate radio 2002; commercial CD single 2003
release_date: Test pressing on pirate radio 2002; single 26 May 2003
tracklist_note: CD: Clean Radio Edit / Remix feat. Wiley & Sharkey Major / Original Mix. Female vocal by Jeanine (Janine) Jacques.

sound_descriptions.text: Opens with a stuttering voice repeating the title, then drops into a bass-heavy rhythm.
Dizzee: built on a dirty bassline and an unfamiliar kick (reused on 'Wot U On?'); strings are his attempt at the strings of 'What's Your Fantasy'.
Boy-girl call-and-response structure modelled on 'Is That Your Chick?' and 'What's Your Fantasy?'.
A 'dark tale' over a bass-heavy instrumental.

context.text: Peaked at no. 29 on the UK Singles Chart (his first top 40) and no. 5 on the UK Indie chart.
The Wire compared its impact on grime to 'Anarchy in the U.K.' for punk; named in The Pitchfork 500 (2008).
Self-produced at 16; made earlier than the rest of Boy in da Corner, after he left college and while on Deja Vu FM and associated with NASTY Crew.
Stereogum: one of the first grime singles to chart in the UK.

relationships.other: I Luv U (Remix) feat. Wiley & Sharkey Major
Dizzee Rascal - Boy in da Corner

title: Boy in da Corner
label: XL Recordings (UK); Matador (US, 2004)
format: Album (LP/CD; formats not itemised in sources opened)
tracklist_note: 15 tracks, 57:08; US edition adds 'Vexed'. Singles: I Luv U, Fix Up Look Sharp, Jus' a Rascal. Recorded Oct 2001 - Mar 2003 at Belly of the Beast and Raskits Lair, London.

sound_descriptions.text: Dizzee says none of the album's tracks is at 140 bpm; the 140 bpm norm came later.
Tracks usually started from drums; samples were spread across a keyboard, one per key; no MPC used.
Entertainment Weekly (via Wikipedia): UK garage beats combined with a distinctly British sensibility; Pitchfork praised its 'cutting sonics'.
Rock edge attributed by Dizzee to grunge and Black Sabbath influences ('Stop Dat').

context.text: Won the 2003 Mercury Prize; peaked at no. 23 on the UK Albums Chart; later certified platinum (BPI, 2018).
Complex (B.J. Steiner) credits it with bringing grime to the rest of the world.
Ranked no. 4 in FACT's 'The 20 best Grime records ever made'.
Made in about a year, when Dizzee was largely unknown outside London pirate radio; he was 18 at release.

relationships.other: I Luv U; Fix Up, Look Sharp; Jus' a Rascal
Round We Go (Chubby Dread beat, originally made for More Fire Crew)

context.text: Peaked at no. 17 on the UK Singles Chart (his first top 20); later certified gold.

title: Functions on the Low
label: White label

sound_descriptions.text: Lo-fi, romantic instrumental (FACT spells it 'Funktions on the Low').
Uses a chipmunked house sample and a 'cheesy synth tone'; melodic interlude.
Five-minute piece of longing; 'neon lights seen through a torrent of tears' (Guardian, Dan Hancox).
Made in about half an hour on FruityLoops.

context.text: Guardian (Dan Hancox): 'quite simply one of the greatest tracks in the history of British electronic music'; XTC (Fuda Guy's older brother) completed only this one track.
Ranked no. 6 in FACT's 'The 20 best Grime records ever made' (white label, 2004).
Described as 'much-mythologised'; original vinyl sells for high prices.
